figures.alt: Photo of an eroding sandy bluff on Lake Michigan with fallen trees at its base and waves washing the shore.
figures.caption: Waves and wind wear the shore away. Erosion moves the pieces.

figures.alt: Photo of a roadside rock cut with thin horizontal layers of tan sandstone and gray shale, and a small white shell lying on one layer.
figures.caption: Rock layers build up over time, usually older at the bottom. A shell fossil is evidence of a past environment.

figures.alt: Photo of a plastic tray with a sand shoreline, a row of stones along part of the shore and a cup of water.
figures.caption: A model shoreline: test a barrier with the same amount of water each time and compare the sediment lost.

figures.alt: Illustration of three people around a plastic shoreline tray: one pours water from a measuring cup, one holds a spoon to measure the sediment and one writes notes.
figures.caption: A shoreline test with the jobs split up: same amount of water every time, then compare the sediment lost.

figures.alt: Interactive: tap a made-up map to find and circle a mountain range, a broad plain and connected lakes.
figures.caption: Find a mountain range, a plain and connected lakes on a map.

figures.alt: Three blue plastic trays in a row, each with a sand bank. The left tray has a big spilled pile of sand, the middle tray has a medium pile with craft sticks beside it, and the right tray has the smallest pile with a small green grass plant. A glass of water stands behind them.
figures.caption: Three model shorelines: no barrier (most sand moved), a wall (some sand moved) and grass (least sand moved). The graph below shows the counts.

figures.alt: Bar graph, Sediment moved by waves. No barrier 12 spoonfuls, Grass 5 spoonfuls, Wall 7 spoonfuls.
figures.caption: Sediment lost in the shoreline tray: no barrier 12 spoonfuls, grass 5 spoonfuls, wall 7 spoonfuls (a teaspoon is about 5 milliliters).
